📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Sources indicate that north Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has lost his race for reelection, a stinging defeat for the man charged with preserving the House majority for the GOP.

Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.

Hudson had already conceded the race Wednesday, when it became clear that his path to victory was closing off.

Sources indicate that “[The] voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice and I respect it,” he said in a statement. “Since 2013 I’ve worked for North Carolina families. That includes the soldiers and families at Fort Bragg, who sacrifice more for this country than most people will ever know.”.

Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose his seat during a midterm election this decade. In 2022, New York Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney lost reelection while serving as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

It has been revealed that republicans across North Carolina experienced devastating losses on election night. As of Thursday afternoon, Democrats had also flipped the seats of Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore, as well as the open seat of retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards. The races for five other GOP-held seats remain uncalled, while Democratic Rep. Don Davis was reelected despite being targeted for defeat under a latest GOP-drawn congressional map. Republicans also lost control of the North Carolina House and lost seats in the state Senate.

Industry observers note that north Carolina’s 9th District, which includes the Eastern Piedmont region and the Fayetteville area, was far from the House battlefield for much of the midterm cycle. President Donald Trump carried the seat by 16 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, and Hudson won a seventh term the same year by nearly 19 points. Hudson also held a financial advantage over Ojeda, raising $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million through mid-October.

But in the waning weeks of the campaign, signs of Republican concern grew and Hudson’s campaign began spending on ads.

Ojeda was first elected to the West Virginia Senate in 2016. He ran for the U.S. House two years later as a Trump-voting Democrat but lost that race to Republican Carol Miller. He then briefly ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and also challenged GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito later that cycle but lost in the Democratic primary.

Ojeda moved to North Carolina in 2020, he told CityView, a local magazine, and he confirmed his challenge to Hudson last year.

Throughout the campaign, he attacked the incumbent over his support for Trump’s agenda, particularly the war in Iran. Ojeda is a retired Army major and the district is home to Fort Bragg, the nation’s largest Army base by population, where the Democrat was previously stationed for more than a decade.

In a recent development, “We did the impossible,’’ Ojeda told supporters Tuesday night. “We took on the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, a man with political connections, the billionaire donors, and the entire Washington establishment standing beside him.”.

Recent findings suggest that hudson, 55, is finishing his seventh term in the House and his second term as NRCC chair. He had no primary opponent this year and had grown used to winning reelection by comfortable margins.

It has been revealed that as a legislator, Hudson focused much of his policy agenda on health challenges such as federal pandemic preparedness programs. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee and chairs the panel's Communications and Technology Subcommittee.

The GTA Files: My Long-Lost Interview With the Brothers Who Founded Rockstar

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, “You can’t fuck with Keith Richards.” That’s what Sam Houser told me when I asked the inspiration for his company name, Rockstar Games.
  • Sources indicate that it was October 2002, just a few weeks before the release of their latest blockbuster, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City.
  • I continued reporting on them and their games during the raucous and turbulent years to follow: hitting over $10 billion in sales, getting compared to Balzac and Dickens in Time magazine, being sued (unsuccessfully) for causing real-life violence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, “You can’t fuck with Keith Richards.” That’s what Sam Houser told me when I asked the inspiration for his company name, Rockstar Games. “I’m a huge fan of the classic golden era of rock stars—both the music, but also the life,” he went on. “You can't argue with Keith Moon riding in a Rolls Royce with a blowup doll hanging out the back and a woman in there screaming, ‘I'm being raped.’ The guy is the original punk rocker. And if we can bring a fraction of that to games, then we’re doing something.”.

Sources indicate that it was October 2002, just a few weeks before the release of their latest blockbuster, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. I’d come to their glossy loft in Soho, Manhattan to interview the elusive 30-year-old Houser and Rockstar co-founders, his younger brother Dan Houser and managing director Terry Donovan, for Rolling Stone. It would be one of their first, last and only in-depth sit-downs together before they decided that the world’s most successful and controversial video game required little explanation from them at all.

I continued reporting on them and their games during the raucous and turbulent years to follow: hitting over $10 billion in sales, getting compared to Balzac and Dickens in Time magazine, being sued (unsuccessfully) for causing real-life violence. As I investigated in my book Jacked: The Outlaw Story of Grand Theft Auto, they also triggered what remains the most outrageous and cinematic scandal ever to hit the industry: the discovery of a hidden sex scene in 2005’s GTA San Andreas that would inspire attempts to legislate and ban the game. As Hilary Clinton noted at the time, “The disturbing material in Grand Theft Auto and other games like it is stealing the innocence of our children and it’s making the difficult job of being a parent even harder.”.

In a recent development, with the gamer generation now grown up and in power, the Reefer Madness panic around GTA has finally given way to something more important: this little game out of Scotland has become the most successful and influential entertainment product of all time. Today, Rockstar returns to Vice City with the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI. More than a decade in the making, with a budget Rockstar has never disclosed but analysts put between $1 billion and $2 billion, the game follows Jason Duval, an ex-soldier, and Lucia Caminos, who phones him from prison, as they’re pulled into a criminal conspiracy across a send-up of Miami. Its first trailer has been viewed more than 300 million times on YouTube, and footage premiering on Netflix nearly crashed the streamer’s servers. Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent manufacturer, expects record revenue of $8.1 billion this fiscal year.

Industry observers note that for longtime fans, GTA 6 marks something more personal: the first game in the franchise since the original band behind it broke up. Following the departure of Donovan and other central figures, Dan Houser exited Rockstar in 2020, leaving his substantial brother Sam as the last founder still there. With Sam remaining notoriously quiet about the new game, I went digging through my old tapes and found my long-lost interview with gaming’s original punk rockers. During our two-hour talk, the young co-founders were brash, unrepentant, and championing a lifetime of obsessions, as Sam put it. “I wasn’t just obsessed about games,” he told me, “we were obsessed about everything—obsessive about music, obsessive about film, obsessive about fashion.”.

GTA 6 highlights that the obsession never left him. Here in this exclusive excerpt from my interview, the Rockstars share how it all started.

It has been revealed that sam Houser: We nearly had a fist fight last week. We have one argument a year.

It has been revealed that sam Houser: That was an old arcade game called Mr. Do! It used to be in like, a bodega, a corner store. You go in there and buy a cigarette for seven P. And you get a couple of games of Mr. Do!. But the games that really got me hooked was when I got into the Sinclair ZX Spectrum. It was very British: a weird little computer with rubber keys, and it was the games that came out then. I was obsessive about everything, really. We had every significant game on every game system going.

Dan Houser: They thought it was interesting. Sam was probably more into games throughout the time. I would come in and out from being interested in them, or being forced to play them. There was physical violence.

Sam Houser: I would beat him into playing.

Terry Donovan: I think for me, there was a period of arcade games: Defender, Track and Field, Tron, Pole Position. So that was that was like the golden age. You would you stand there and if a bloke lasted two hours on 10p on Defender, you thought he was it. If you grew up in the '70s, you probably wanted to be a guitarist. If you were in the '80s, you probably wanted to be a DJ. The things you grow up wanting now, you probably want to be a video game designer.

Sam Houser: Absolutely. That’s one of the essential things, for me, in games. Look at the games we do now. The game that really coined that in the early days, particularly for me, was this game Elite. You were a space smuggler, and it was just very simple graphics—black screen with just white lights on it. And you flew around space, interacting with other spaceships and other colonies and other planets and so on.

Dan Houser: It's like reading any kind of book when you're a kid or anything that makes you feel like you're not in the real world.

Recent findings suggest that sam Houser: What was interesting about GTA 1 was that graphically it was top down. It wasn't as sharp or appealing as things that were popular at the time, like Tomb Raider and all these other games that were coming out. You were put into the world, and you were given choices. It was a very sort of non-linear experience. Because it highlighted all these people out there that wanted this kind of experience that were prepared to forego the graphical gratification you got at the Tomb Raider—you know, that girl with the nice breasts. Suddenly you were playing in 2D and it was top down. It was utterly compelling.

I thought the subject matter was a really appealing hook. We felt that the sort of the fantasy sci-fi, fantasy, you know, Dungeons & Dragons, and here's my sword and there's that orc. We didn't feel that the mass market was that into that stuff. We wanted to make things that felt a little bit more relevant to people like ourselves. The reason it sold is it was incredibly fun to play. It was originally called Race n' Chase. Kind of catchy name. In the UK, the game was in the House of Parliament, and it got a massive share of media attention. It was on BBC News five times in one day. Like, oh my God!

It has been revealed that terry Donovan: It was one first piece of entertainment that was sort of unashamed antihero. There's no twist at the end where he turns out to be a good guy.

Industry observers note that dan Houser: Freedom was the thing that appealed. Because as free as games like Defender and Scramble were for us, 10 years on, they felt restrictive. I don't consider myself a master gamer. I play every game. I'm good at them. But I think that we try and make games that can be played by normal folk as well as hardcore too. And the problem with some of those other games is when you hit a point that's frustrating, you can't get past it. But in Grand Theft Auto, any of them, when you hit a point that's tough, you just go and do something else. And then while you're doing the other thing, you're thinking about this other thing that you've been stuck on, and then you come back to it and crack it. I think that's fucking great.

Sam Houser: I came out here and did a very energetic pitch where I must have sweated through three layers of clothing in my kind of insanely sweaty way, and everyone in the office was like, "Who the fuck is that guy?".

Sam Houser: They just didn't want it. Business is so like, “What's that person doing? We must copy that.” Everybody else was doing 3D platform games and 3D sports games, all these shooters.

Industry observers note that sam Houser: I first came here in my 18th birthday. It my 18th birthday present or whatever to just go and buy leather hip-hop puffers and Air Jordan Mark V's. From that moment I was chronically in love with the place. The idea that I would end up here making games where games is traditionally a West Coast thing, to me it's just like… in some ways I feel it was meant to be. We were kind of enlisted to sort of build that.

Sam Houser: The mission was basically to bring our attitude, to try and make games that felt more relevant to the audience that was playing.

It has been revealed that dan Houser: It’s more modern, more accessible, gameplay over graphics, but with a slightly anarchic, edgy fantasy—a fantasy you would have walking down the street rather than from reading Dungeons & Dragons. It’s a fantasy where you're a street racer rather than a wizard.

Terry Donovan: [to Sam] How much did you want a Def Jam baseball jacket?

According to recent reports, sam Houser: More than anything in the world. They had this attitude: “Here's where we from. Here's what we do. If you don't like us, fuck you. Everything we touch is somehow made more magical.” A guy like Rick Rubin is such a fucking hero, because you go from doing the hip-hop that he pioneered to doing Slayer, to doing The Cult.

Sam Houser: We call it The Commune.

Industry observers note that terry Donovan: It was a first-floor apartment on Water Street, in the South Street Seaport, and it had glass on the front. There was no fucking light in it.

Sam Houser: There was about 20 people. By the time I was in there, there was about seven people living in there. That whole teenager-in-the-bedroom-with-the-bottle-top-specs thing comes around the games industry like a fucking albatross. This wasn't the kind of lonely nine-year-old or 12-year-old kid, or the one who's going to end up exposing himself to schoolgirl doing this.

Terry Donovan: The lines are our decision of what's funny and what's tasteful. What isn't relevant to what a lot of what other people think. If you think it's funny, you put it in your machine, if you don't think it's funny, you don't.
